flashcards.q: Mechanically, why does cross-lingual retrieval work with no translation step at query time?
flashcards.a: Multilingual embedding models train with a contrastive objective over cross-lingual pairs known/inferred to share meaning, pulling translation-equivalent text together in vector space regardless of language. The model never distinguished "similar because same language" from "similar because same meaning" -- it only optimized for the latter.

flashcards.q: What is tokenizer fertility, and why is it an operational cost, not just a linguistic footnote?
flashcards.a: Fertility is tokens produced per word (or per character for non-whitespace scripts). Non-English, especially morphologically rich or non-Latin-script languages, routinely need 1.5-2x+ the tokens for equivalent content -- a direct cost/latency tax on embedding, chunking, and generation, not merely a quality nuance.

flashcards.q: Does lower tokenizer fertility always predict better model performance for that language?
flashcards.a: No. A 2025 70-language study found fertility alone explains relatively little of the variance in downstream performance -- it's a real cost signal but not a complete quality proxy.

flashcards.q: Why is a single blended recall@k metric dangerous for a 22-locale product?
flashcards.a: One language's retrieval can collapse to near-zero while being mathematically absorbed by 21 other healthy languages, leaving the blended number flat. The failure typically surfaces via support tickets weeks later, not monitoring.

flashcards.q: What is the structural fix for the silent per-locale degradation failure?
flashcards.a: Report and alert on recall@k/nDCG PER LOCALE as a hard requirement, not only blended -- a golden set stratified by language with independent alerting thresholds per locale.

flashcards.q: Compare shared multilingual index vs. per-language index, with the real cost of each.
flashcards.a: Shared index: simpler (one index, one model) but risks cross-lingual leakage that a blended metric hides. Per-language index: isolates quality, allows language-specific models, but costs N indexes to build/monitor/reindex, multiplying every ops task by locale count.

flashcards.q: What's the practical default for shared vs. per-language indexing at scale?
flashcards.a: Shared index with language-aware routing/metadata filtering as the default, moving to per-language handling only for specific locales where per-locale evaluation shows the shared model measurably underperforms.

flashcards.q: Why does a whitespace tokenizer fail on Japanese or Chinese text for lexical retrieval?
flashcards.a: CJK scripts have no whitespace between words. A whitespace tokenizer either treats each character as its own token (destroying multi-character word meaning BM25 depends on) or fails to segment at all. A dedicated segmenter (Jieba for Chinese, MeCab for Japanese) is required.

flashcards.q: What happens by default when a user types a romanized query for a non-Latin-script language, and what's the fix?
flashcards.a: Nothing matches -- the index holds native-script content and the romanized query shares no tokens or embedding proximity unless the model incidentally learned transliteration robustness. Fix: normalize via transliteration at index or query time, or select/fine-tune a model with demonstrated transliteration robustness.

flashcards.q: How should mixed-language (code-switched) queries be handled by language detection and routing?
flashcards.a: Use top-k language predictions, not top-1. On low-confidence or closely-contested top-2, either run retrieval across both candidate languages and fuse, or fall back to the shared multilingual embedding space directly, since it doesn't require a language label to function.

flashcards.q: What is fastText lid.176 and what are its performance characteristics?
flashcards.a: A language identification model trained on Wikipedia/Tatoeba/SETimes data covering 176 languages. Compressed .ftz variant is under 1MB, reports F1 in the high-0.9s on clean single-language text, fast enough to run per-query with negligible latency.

flashcards.q: Why might a language advertised inside a "100+ languages supported" embedding model still underperform?
flashcards.a: Aggregate language-count claims say nothing about per-language training data volume; low-resource languages sit in the weaker tail of the same model's coverage by construction. Validate per-locale against your own golden set rather than trusting the vendor's headline claim.

flashcards.q: When does translate-then-retrieve still beat a multilingual embedding model in 2026?
flashcards.a: For a genuinely low-resource language where the multilingual embedding's cross-lingual alignment is weak due to insufficient training data -- the translation model may have more effective signal for that language pair than the embedding does.
